items.title: Gradient descent
items.explainer: Most machine-learning models are trained by minimizing a loss function: a single number that measures how wrong the model's predictions are on the training data. Gradient descent is the workhorse algorithm for this job. The gradient of the loss with respect to the model's parameters points in the direction in which the loss increases fastest, so the algorithm takes a small step in the opposite direction, recomputes the gradient, and repeats until the loss stops improving. The size of each step is set by the learning rate. If the learning rate is too large, updates overshoot the minimum and the loss oscillates or even diverges; if it is too small, training becomes painfully slow and can stall on flat regions of the loss surface. Computing the exact gradient over an entire data set at every step is expensive, so stochastic gradient descent (SGD) estimates it from a small random mini-batch of examples instead. That estimate is noisy but cheap, and the noise can even help the optimizer escape shallow local minima. Refinements such as momentum and Adam adapt the step size for each parameter, and they are the default optimizers behind most modern neural networks.

question.prompt: In gradient descent, what is the most likely effect of setting the learning rate far too high?

options.text: Updates overshoot the minimum, so the loss oscillates or diverges
Training converges faster and more reliably
The gradient becomes exactly zero after one step
The optimizer automatically switches to mini-batches

question.explanation: A large learning rate makes each step jump past the minimum; successive steps can bounce back and forth or grow, so the loss oscillates or diverges instead of settling.

items.title: Overfitting and the bias-variance trade-off
items.explainer: A model overfits when it learns the noise and quirks of its training data instead of the underlying pattern. The symptom is a large gap between performance on the training set, which looks excellent, and performance on new data, which is much worse. The bias-variance trade-off gives a precise way to think about this. For squared-error loss, the expected error of a prediction on a new point splits into three parts: squared bias, the error from wrong assumptions such as fitting a straight line to a curved relationship; variance, the sensitivity of the fitted model to the particular training sample it happened to see; and irreducible noise in the outcome itself. Simple models tend to have high bias and low variance, while very flexible models have low bias and high variance. As model complexity grows, test error therefore often traces a U-shape: falling at first as bias shrinks, then rising as variance takes over. Standard remedies are more training data, regularization, early stopping, and using cross-validation to choose the complexity. Very large neural networks complicate this classical picture: they can show 'double descent', where test error falls again once a model has enough capacity to fit the training data perfectly.

question.prompt: A model has 1% error on its training data but 25% error on held-out data. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: High bias (underfitting)
High variance (overfitting)
Irreducible noise only
A learning rate that is too small

question.explanation: Near-perfect training performance with much worse held-out performance means the model fits its specific sample too closely: the signature of high variance, i.e., overfitting.

items.title: Backpropagation
items.explainer: Training a neural network with gradient descent requires the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight, and a large network can have billions of them. Backpropagation computes all of these gradients efficiently by applying the chain rule of calculus systematically. In the forward pass, the input flows through the network layer by layer and each layer's intermediate values are stored. In the backward pass, the algorithm starts from the derivative of the loss at the output and works back toward the input, multiplying by each layer's local derivative to obtain the gradient for that layer's weights. Because intermediate results are reused rather than recomputed, the whole backward pass costs only a small constant multiple of the forward pass. In modern terms, backpropagation is reverse-mode automatic differentiation, which frameworks such as PyTorch and JAX perform automatically. The method was popularized for neural networks by Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams in 1986. A well-known difficulty is the vanishing gradient: multiplying many factors smaller than one through a deep stack of layers shrinks the gradient reaching the early layers, so they barely learn. ReLU activations, careful weight initialization, normalization layers and residual connections were all developed partly to counter this effect.
items.formula: \frac{\partial L}{\partial w} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial a} \cdot \frac{\partial a}{\partial z} \cdot \frac{\partial z}{\partial w}

question.prompt: Why do very deep networks without residual connections or careful initialization often suffer from vanishing gradients?

options.text: Backpropagation skips the early layers to save time
The forward pass discards activations before the backward pass
The chain rule multiplies many factors smaller than one, shrinking the gradient in early layers
The loss function becomes non-differentiable in deep networks

question.explanation: Each layer contributes a multiplicative factor to the gradient. When many of those factors are below one, their product shrinks toward zero by the time it reaches the first layers.

items.title: Self-attention and the transformer
items.explainer: The transformer architecture, introduced in the 2017 paper 'Attention Is All You Need', underlies today's large language models. Its core operation is self-attention. Each token's representation is projected into three vectors: a query, a key and a value. The attention weight from one token to another is computed from the dot product of the first token's query with the second token's key, scaled by the square root of the key dimension and normalized with a softmax across all tokens. Each token's output is then the weighted average of all the value vectors. This lets every token draw information directly from every other token in a single step, however far apart they are, whereas recurrent networks had to pass information along the sequence one position at a time. Because all positions are processed in parallel, transformers train efficiently on GPUs. Two details matter in practice. First, multi-head attention runs several attention operations side by side so the model can track different kinds of relationships at once. Second, attention by itself ignores word order, so positional encodings are added to the token embeddings. The main cost is that attention compares every pair of tokens, so compute grows quadratically with sequence length.

source.title: Vaswani et al. (2017), Attention Is All You Need - arXiv

question.prompt: Why do transformers add positional encodings to token embeddings?

options.text: To reduce the size of the vocabulary
To make the cost of attention grow linearly with length
To replace the value vectors in attention
Self-attention on its own is insensitive to the order of tokens

question.explanation: Attention computes weighted averages over a set of tokens; shuffling the tokens would give the same result. Positional encodings inject order information so 'dog bites man' differs from 'man bites dog'.

items.title: Tokenization and byte-pair encoding
items.explainer: Language models do not read text as letters or as whole words. Text is first split into tokens drawn from a fixed vocabulary, and the model only ever sees sequences of token IDs. The most common way to build that vocabulary is byte-pair encoding (BPE). It starts from individual characters or bytes, counts which adjacent pair occurs most often in a large training corpus, merges that pair into a new token, and repeats the process until the vocabulary reaches a target size, often tens of thousands of tokens or more. Frequent words end up as single tokens, while rare words are broken into smaller subword pieces, so no input is ever completely out of vocabulary. BPE began as a data-compression technique in the 1990s and was adapted for neural machine translation in 2016. Tokenization has visible consequences. Model context limits and API prices are counted in tokens rather than words. Languages that were underrepresented in the tokenizer's training data need more tokens per word, which makes them slower and costlier to process. And tasks that depend on individual letters, such as counting the r's in a word or reversing a string, are harder than they look, because the model sees chunks of characters rather than the letters themselves.

question.prompt: Under byte-pair encoding, how is a rare word that never appeared during vocabulary training usually handled?

options.text: It is split into smaller subword tokens that are in the vocabulary
It is replaced with a single 'unknown' token
It is silently dropped from the input
The tokenizer retrains itself on the new word

question.explanation: Because the vocabulary is built up from single characters or bytes, any string can be represented as a sequence of smaller known pieces.

items.title: Embeddings
items.explainer: An embedding maps a discrete item, such as a word, a token, a product or a user, to a dense vector of real numbers, typically with a few hundred to a few thousand dimensions. The vectors are learned so that items that appear in similar contexts or play similar roles end up close together in that space. Closeness is usually measured with cosine similarity, which compares the directions of two vectors while ignoring their lengths. The word2vec models of 2013 made embeddings famous by showing that simple vector arithmetic could capture relationships: the vector for 'king' minus 'man' plus 'woman' lands near the vector for 'queen'. Today embeddings power semantic search, where a query and a collection of documents are embedded and the nearest documents are retrieved even if they share no exact words with the query. They also drive recommendation systems, clustering, duplicate detection, and retrieval-augmented generation, in which relevant passages are fetched and handed to a language model as context. One caution: embeddings absorb the statistical patterns of their training data, including social biases. Early word embeddings, for example, placed many occupations closer to one gender than the other, mirroring the text they were trained on.

question.prompt: In a semantic search system, what does a high cosine similarity between a query embedding and a document embedding indicate?

options.text: The document is longer than the query
The vectors point in similar directions, suggesting similar meaning
The document contains every word of the query
The two vectors have exactly the same length

question.explanation: Cosine similarity measures the angle between vectors, not their length or word overlap. A value near 1 means the embeddings point the same way, which the model learned to associate with related meaning.

items.title: Cross-validation
items.explainer: A model's error on the data it was trained on is an overly optimistic guide to how it will perform on new data. Cross-validation gives a more honest estimate. In k-fold cross-validation, the data set is split into k roughly equal parts, or folds. The model is trained on k minus 1 folds and evaluated on the remaining fold, and this is repeated k times so that every fold serves as the test set exactly once. The k error estimates are then averaged. Common choices are k equal to 5 or 10. Compared with a single train-test split, cross-validation uses all the data for both training and evaluation and gives a less noisy estimate, which makes it the standard tool for choosing hyperparameters such as regularization strength or tree depth. Three pitfalls are common. First, data leakage: any preprocessing that learns from data, such as scaling or feature selection, must be fit inside each training fold, never on the full data set. Second, time series: random folds let the model train on the future, so forward-chaining splits are needed. Third, grouped data: if one patient contributes several samples, all of them must stay in the same fold.

question.prompt: A team standardizes all features using the mean and standard deviation of the full data set, then runs 10-fold cross-validation. What is the problem?

options.text: Ten folds is too many for most data sets
Standardization is never allowed before model fitting
Information from the held-out folds leaks into training, making the estimate optimistic
Cross-validation only works for classification problems

question.explanation: The scaling statistics were computed using the test folds, so each model has indirectly seen its evaluation data. Preprocessing must be fit within each training fold.

items.title: Regularization: L1 and L2 penalties
items.explainer: Regularization discourages a model from fitting noise by adding a penalty on the size of its parameters to the loss being minimized. The two classic penalties behave differently. L2 regularization, used in ridge regression and called weight decay in deep learning, adds the sum of squared weights. It shrinks all weights smoothly toward zero but rarely makes any of them exactly zero. L1 regularization, used in the lasso, adds the sum of absolute values of the weights. Because of the sharp corner of the absolute-value function at zero, it tends to push some weights exactly to zero, so it also performs feature selection and yields sparse, easier-to-interpret models. The elastic net combines both penalties. The penalty strength, often written lambda, controls the trade-off: larger values mean simpler models with more bias and less variance. It is usually chosen by cross-validation. Regularization also has a Bayesian reading: minimizing the L2-penalized loss is equivalent to finding the most probable weights under a Gaussian prior, and the L1 penalty corresponds to a Laplace prior. In deep learning, dropout, early stopping and data augmentation serve as additional regularizers that limit overfitting without an explicit penalty term.

question.prompt: Which penalty tends to set some coefficients exactly to zero, performing feature selection?

options.text: L2 penalty (ridge regression)
Dropout
No penalty (ordinary least squares)
L1 penalty (lasso)

question.explanation: The L1 penalty's corner at zero makes zero an attractive solution for weak features, so the lasso drops them entirely. Ridge only shrinks coefficients toward zero.

items.title: Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF)
items.explainer: A pretrained language model is trained to predict the next token of internet text, which is not the same as being helpful, honest or safe. Reinforcement learning from human feedback is one of the main techniques used to close that gap. It typically runs in three stages. First, the model is fine-tuned on examples of good responses written by people. Second, people compare pairs of model responses to the same prompt, and a separate reward model is trained to predict which response they prefer. Third, the language model is optimized with a reinforcement-learning algorithm, commonly proximal policy optimization (PPO), to produce responses that the reward model scores highly. A penalty on the KL divergence from the original model keeps the tuned model from drifting too far, which limits reward hacking: producing text that scores well with the reward model without actually being better. The approach was popularized for instruction-following models in 2022. Newer methods simplify or extend it. Direct preference optimization (DPO) learns from the preference pairs without a separate reward model or reinforcement-learning loop, and AI-feedback methods such as Constitutional AI use model judgments guided by written principles. A known limitation is that optimizing for human approval can reward flattery over accuracy.

source.title: Reinforcement learning from human feedback - Wikipedia

question.prompt: What is the main purpose of the KL-divergence penalty in RLHF fine-tuning?

options.text: To keep the tuned model close to the reference model, limiting reward hacking and degenerate outputs
To speed up training by skipping the reward model
To train the reward model from human comparisons
To reduce the size of the tokenizer vocabulary

question.explanation: Without the penalty, the policy can exploit flaws in the learned reward model and drift into odd text. The KL term anchors it to the original model's distribution.

items.title: Convolutional neural networks
items.explainer: Convolutional neural networks, or CNNs, are designed for data arranged on a grid, above all images. Instead of connecting every input pixel to every unit in the next layer, a convolutional layer slides small learnable filters, often 3 by 3 pixels, across the image. Each filter responds to a particular local pattern, such as an edge at a certain angle, wherever that pattern appears. Because the same filter weights are reused at every position, a convolutional layer needs far fewer parameters than a fully connected layer, and a feature learned in one corner of an image is automatically recognized in the others. Stacking layers builds a hierarchy: early layers detect edges and colors, middle layers detect textures and parts, and deeper layers respond to whole objects. Pooling or strided convolutions shrink the spatial resolution along the way, so each unit in a deep layer sees a large region of the original image. The 2012 ImageNet competition, won decisively by the CNN known as AlexNet, is widely seen as the moment deep learning took over computer vision. Vision transformers now rival CNNs on many benchmarks, but CNNs remain widespread, especially on phones and other devices with limited compute.
items.formula: (I * K)(i, j) = \sum_{m} \sum_{n} I(i + m,\, j + n)\, K(m, n)

question.prompt: Why does a convolutional layer need far fewer parameters than a fully connected layer on the same image?

options.text: It ignores the color channels of the image
The same small filter weights are reused at every position in the image
It only processes the center of the image
It has no bias terms

question.explanation: Weight sharing means one 3x3 filter has just nine weights per channel, applied everywhere, instead of a separate weight for every pixel-to-unit connection.

items.title: Dropout regularization
items.explainer: Dropout is a simple trick for reducing overfitting in neural networks. During each training step, every neuron in a chosen layer is switched off at random with some probability, often 10 to 50 percent, so its output is set to zero for that step. The network therefore cannot rely on any single neuron or on fragile combinations of neurons that only work together. Instead it is pushed to spread useful information across many units, which makes the learned features more robust. A helpful way to picture dropout is as training a huge ensemble of thinned networks that share weights, then averaging them at test time. At test time nothing is dropped; instead the activations are scaled so their expected size matches what the next layer saw during training. Most libraries do this scaling during training instead, a variant called inverted dropout, so inference code stays unchanged. Dropout was introduced by Geoffrey Hinton's group around 2012 and helped deep networks win image recognition contests. It is less common in convolutional layers today, where batch normalization and data augmentation do similar work, but it remains standard in fully connected layers and in transformers, which apply dropout to attention weights and residual connections.

question.prompt: What happens to dropout at test time in a standard network?

options.text: Neurons are still dropped at random, so predictions vary
The dropped neurons are permanently removed
Nothing is dropped; activations are scaled so their expected size matches training
The dropout rate is doubled to compensate

question.explanation: At inference every unit is active; scaling keeps the expected input to the next layer the same as during training (inverted dropout does the scaling during training instead).

items.title: Batch normalization
items.explainer: Batch normalization is a layer that rescales the activations flowing through a neural network so they have a stable distribution. For each mini-batch during training, it computes the mean and variance of every feature, subtracts the mean and divides by the standard deviation, so the feature has roughly zero mean and unit variance. It then multiplies by a learned scale and adds a learned shift, so the network can still represent whatever distribution works best. Introduced by Sergey Ioffe and Christian Szegedy in 2015, it made deep networks train faster and tolerate higher learning rates. The original motivation was to reduce internal covariate shift, the changing distribution of inputs to each layer as earlier layers learn; later research suggests its main benefit is that it smooths the loss landscape, making gradients more predictable. At inference time the batch statistics are replaced by running averages collected during training, so a single example gives a deterministic output. Batch normalization works poorly with very small batches, because the estimated statistics become noisy. Layer normalization, which normalizes across the features of a single example instead of across the batch, avoids this problem and is the standard choice in transformers.

question.prompt: Why do transformers usually use layer normalization rather than batch normalization?

options.text: Layer normalization has no learned parameters
Batch normalization cannot be used with attention mathematically
Layer normalization makes the model smaller
Layer normalization does not depend on batch statistics, so it works with any batch size and sequence length

question.explanation: Layer normalization normalizes across the features of each example, so it avoids the noisy and batch-dependent statistics that hurt batch normalization.

items.title: Recurrent neural networks and LSTMs
items.explainer: A recurrent neural network processes a sequence one element at a time while carrying a hidden state, a vector that summarizes what it has seen so far. At each step the same weights combine the current input with the previous hidden state to produce a new one, so the network can in principle remember information across long sequences such as sentences, audio or sensor data. In practice simple recurrent networks struggle to learn long-range dependencies, because gradients passed back through many steps either shrink towards zero or blow up, the vanishing and exploding gradient problems. The long short-term memory network, or LSTM, proposed by Sepp Hochreiter and Jürgen Schmidhuber in 1997, addresses this with a separate cell state and three gates. The forget gate decides what to erase from memory, the input gate decides what new information to store, and the output gate decides what to reveal as the hidden state. Because information can flow along the cell state with little change, gradients survive over many more steps. LSTMs powered speech recognition and machine translation in the 2010s. Transformers have since replaced them for most language tasks, because attention processes all positions in parallel, which trains far faster on modern hardware.

question.prompt: What problem were LSTM gates mainly designed to solve?

options.text: Vanishing gradients that prevent learning long-range dependencies
Networks being too large to fit in memory
The need for labeled training data
Slow inference on graphics processors

question.explanation: The cell state and gates let information and gradients flow across many time steps, which plain recurrent networks fail to do.

items.title: Precision, recall and the F1 score
items.explainer: Accuracy, the share of predictions that are correct, can be badly misleading when one class is rare. A fraud detector that labels every transaction as legitimate may be 99.9 percent accurate and completely useless. Precision and recall look at the positive class directly. Precision asks: of all the cases the model flagged as positive, how many really were positive? Recall asks: of all the truly positive cases, how many did the model find? A cautious model that flags only the most obvious cases has high precision but low recall; an aggressive one that flags anything suspicious has high recall but low precision. Most classifiers output a score, and moving the decision threshold trades one against the other. The F1 score combines the two into a single number using the harmonic mean, which is low whenever either precision or recall is low, so a model cannot score well by maximizing only one. Which metric matters depends on the cost of mistakes. Missing a cancer on a screening scan is worse than a false alarm, so recall is prioritized; a spam filter that hides real email is costly, so precision matters more. Precision-recall curves show the trade-off across every threshold.

question.prompt: A model flags 50 transactions as fraud; 40 of them are fraud, and 100 frauds exist in total. What are its precision and recall?

options.text: Precision 0.4, recall 0.8
Precision 0.8, recall 0.4
Precision 0.5, recall 0.4
Precision 0.8, recall 0.5

question.explanation: Precision is 40 of 50 flagged (0.8); recall is 40 of the 100 real frauds (0.4).

items.title: Decision trees and random forests
items.explainer: A decision tree makes predictions by asking a sequence of yes-or-no questions about the input, such as whether income is above a threshold or whether a symptom is present. Each answer leads down a branch until a leaf gives the prediction. Trees are learned by repeatedly choosing the split that best separates the training examples, measured by criteria such as Gini impurity or information gain. They are easy to interpret, need little data preparation and handle mixed numeric and categorical features. Their weakness is variance: a single deep tree can memorize noise, and a small change in the data can produce a very different tree. A random forest, introduced by Leo Breiman in 2001, fixes this by growing hundreds of trees and averaging their votes. Each tree is trained on a bootstrap sample of the data, drawn with replacement, and at each split it may only consider a random subset of features. These two sources of randomness make the trees different from one another, so their errors partly cancel when averaged. Random forests are strong default models for tabular data, rarely overfit badly and give useful estimates of feature importance. Gradient-boosted trees, which add trees one at a time to correct earlier errors, often do even better.

question.prompt: Why does a random forest train each tree on a bootstrap sample and a random subset of features?

options.text: To make every tree identical
To reduce the number of trees needed to one
To make the trees differ, so their errors partly cancel when averaged
To guarantee zero training error

question.explanation: Averaging works best when the models are not all making the same mistakes; randomness decorrelates the trees.

items.title: k-means clustering
items.explainer: k-means is a classic method for grouping unlabeled data into k clusters. You choose k in advance. The algorithm starts by placing k centroids, often at randomly chosen data points. It then alternates two steps. In the assignment step, every point joins the cluster of its nearest centroid. In the update step, each centroid moves to the mean of the points assigned to it. The steps repeat until assignments stop changing. Each round can only lower the total squared distance between points and their centroids, so the algorithm always converges, but only to a local optimum that depends on the starting positions. In practice it is run several times with different starts, and the k-means++ method spreads the initial centroids out to improve results. k-means assumes clusters are roughly round and of similar size, because it measures plain Euclidean distance to a single center. It struggles with elongated or nested shapes and is sensitive to features on different scales, so data is usually standardized first. Choosing k is a judgement call; the elbow method plots the total within-cluster distance against k and looks for the point where adding clusters stops helping much. Uses range from customer segmentation to compressing the colors in an image.

question.prompt: Why is k-means usually run several times with different starting centroids?

options.text: Each run uses a different k automatically
A single run never converges
Running it once overfits the labels
It converges only to a local optimum that depends on the starting positions

question.explanation: Different initializations can end in different local optima; keeping the best of several runs gives a better clustering.

items.title: Principal component analysis
items.explainer: Principal component analysis, or PCA, reduces many correlated variables to a few new ones that keep most of the information. It finds the direction in the data along which the points vary the most; that is the first principal component. The second component is the direction of greatest remaining variance at right angles to the first, and so on. Mathematically, the components are the eigenvectors of the data's covariance matrix, and each eigenvalue says how much variance its component captures. Projecting the data onto the first few components gives a compact representation: a dataset with hundreds of gene-expression measurements per sample can often be summarized by two or three components that separate the main groups. PCA is used for visualization, for removing noise, and as a preprocessing step that speeds up other algorithms. It has limits. It only finds linear structure, so curved relationships need other methods such as t-SNE or UMAP for visualization. It is sensitive to scale, so variables are usually standardized first, otherwise a variable measured in large units dominates. And the components are mixtures of the original variables, which can make them hard to interpret. The method goes back to Karl Pearson in 1901 and Harold Hotelling in 1933.

question.prompt: What does the first principal component of a dataset represent?

options.text: The direction along which the data varies the most
The variable with the largest mean
The cluster containing the most points
The variable least correlated with the others

question.explanation: The first component is the direction of maximum variance; later components capture the remaining variance at right angles.

items.title: Generative adversarial networks
items.explainer: A generative adversarial network, or GAN, learns to create realistic data by setting two neural networks against each other. The generator takes random noise and tries to turn it into a convincing sample, such as a photo of a face. The discriminator receives a mix of real samples and generated ones and tries to tell them apart. The two are trained together: the discriminator is rewarded for spotting fakes, and the generator is rewarded for fooling the discriminator. As each improves, the other must improve too, and in the ideal case the generator ends up producing samples the discriminator cannot distinguish from real data. Ian Goodfellow and colleagues introduced GANs in 2014, and later versions such as StyleGAN produced photorealistic faces of people who do not exist. GANs are fast at generating images, needing only one pass through the generator. They are also notoriously hard to train. The balance between the two networks can collapse, and in mode collapse the generator learns to produce only a few kinds of output that reliably fool the discriminator, ignoring the variety in the real data. Diffusion models, which train more stably and cover the data more fully, have since overtaken GANs for most image generation.

question.prompt: What is mode collapse in a GAN?

options.text: The discriminator stops training
The generator produces only a few kinds of output instead of the full variety of the data
The network runs out of memory
Generated images become identical to the training images

question.explanation: In mode collapse the generator settles on a narrow set of outputs that fool the discriminator, losing diversity.

items.title: Diffusion models
items.explainer: Diffusion models generate images, audio and other data by learning to reverse a gradual noising process. In the forward process, a training image is corrupted over many small steps by adding Gaussian noise until nothing but noise remains. A neural network, usually a U-Net or a transformer, is trained to undo one step: given a noisy image and the step number, it predicts the noise that was added. Generation runs this in reverse. Starting from pure noise, the model repeatedly removes a little predicted noise, and an image emerges over tens to hundreds of steps. Because each training example only asks the network to predict noise at a random step, training is stable and covers the variety of the data well, avoiding the mode collapse that troubles GANs. To control what is generated, the network is also given a condition, such as a text embedding, and classifier-free guidance strengthens the condition by comparing predictions with and without it. Running the process in a compressed latent space, as Stable Diffusion does, cuts the cost dramatically. The main drawback is speed, since many network evaluations are needed per sample, and much research aims to reduce the number of steps, for example with distillation.

question.prompt: During training, what is a diffusion model's network typically asked to predict?

options.text: The class label of the image
The next pixel in raster order
The noise that was added to a noisy image at a given step
Whether the image is real or fake

question.explanation: The network learns to predict the added noise; generation then removes predicted noise step by step from pure noise.

items.title: Retrieval-augmented generation
items.explainer: Retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG, lets a language model answer questions using documents it was never trained on. Before the model writes an answer, a retrieval step searches a collection of documents for passages relevant to the question, and those passages are inserted into the prompt. The model then answers from the supplied text rather than from memory alone. The collection is usually prepared by splitting documents into chunks and converting each chunk into an embedding, a vector that captures its meaning; the question is embedded the same way, and the chunks whose vectors are closest are retrieved. Keyword search is often combined with this vector search, and a reranking model may reorder the results. RAG has practical advantages. Knowledge can be updated by changing the documents instead of retraining the model, answers can cite their sources, and private data stays in a store the organization controls. It reduces but does not eliminate made-up answers, because the model may still ignore or misread the retrieved text, and a poor retrieval step returns the wrong passages, which no model can fix. Results depend heavily on how documents are chunked, what embedding model is used and how many passages are included.

question.prompt: What is a key advantage of retrieval-augmented generation over retraining a model on new documents?

options.text: It makes the model smaller
It removes the need for a language model
It guarantees that answers are always correct
Knowledge can be updated by changing the document store, without retraining

question.explanation: RAG supplies current documents at question time, so updating knowledge means updating the store; it does not guarantee correctness.
